‘Now,’ said Mr. Lorry, gently resting his hand on the Doctor’s arm again after they had both been silent for a moment, ‘what would you say caused this attack?’

‘I believe,’ Doctor Manette replied, ‘that the thoughts and memories responsible for the original illness had returned with unusual force. Certain intensely distressing associations had been vividly brought back to him, I think. He had probably been carrying a fear of their return for a long time—under particular circumstances, perhaps, or on one specific occasion. He tried unsuccessfully to prepare himself. Perhaps that effort itself made him less able to endure it.’

‘Would he remember what happened during the relapse?’ Mr. Lorry asked, understandably hesitant.

The Doctor looked bleakly around the room, shook his head, and answered quietly, ‘Nothing at all.’

‘And as for the future?’ Mr. Lorry suggested.

‘As for the future,’ said the Doctor, regaining his steadiness, ‘I would be very hopeful. Since Heaven has mercifully restored him so quickly, I would have great hope. He gave way under the pressure of something complicated, something he had long dreaded, vaguely foreseen, and struggled against. Now he has recovered after the storm broke and passed. I would hope that the worst is behind him.’

‘Well, well! That is reassuring. I’m grateful!’ said Mr. Lorry.

‘I’m grateful!’ the Doctor repeated, bowing his head reverently.

‘There are two more things,’ Mr. Lorry said, ‘that I’m anxious to understand. May I continue?’

‘You could do nothing better for your friend.’ The Doctor offered him his hand.

‘The first, then. He is a studious man with unusual energy. He works passionately at expanding his professional knowledge, conducting experiments, and many other things. Could he be doing too much?’

‘I don’t think so. His mind may have an unusually strong need to stay occupied. That might be partly natural to him and partly a consequence of his suffering. The less it has healthy subjects to engage with, the greater the danger of its turning towards unhealthy ones. He may have discovered this by observing himself.’

‘You’re certain he isn’t putting himself under too much strain?’

‘I believe I can be quite certain.’

‘My dear Manette, if he were overworked, though—’

‘My dear Lorry, I doubt that would be easy. There has been tremendous pressure in one direction, and something is needed to balance it.’

‘Forgive a businessman’s persistence. Suppose for a moment that he was overworked: would that show itself through some return of this disorder?’

At the sight of it, the orangutan immediately sprang through the bedroom door, raced downstairs, and escaped into the street through a window that had unfortunately been left open.

The Frenchman pursued it desperately. Still holding the razor, the ape occasionally stopped to look back and gesture at him until he was almost within reach, then darted away again. The chase continued like this for a long time. It was nearly three in the morning, and the streets were completely silent. As they passed along an alley behind the Rue Morgue, a light shining from the open window of Madame L’Espanaye’s fourth-floor bedroom caught the animal’s attention. It rushed to the house, spotted the lightning rod, and climbed it with astonishing agility. Gripping the shutter, which had been folded fully back against the wall, it used it to swing straight onto the bed’s headboard. The entire feat took less than a minute. As it entered the room, the orangutan kicked the shutter open again.

Meanwhile, the sailor felt both relief and uncertainty. He now had a strong chance of recapturing the animal, since it could hardly escape the trap it had entered except by descending the rod, where he could intercept it. But the thought of what it might do inside the house gave him serious cause for alarm. This concern drove him to keep following it. Climbing a lightning rod presents little difficulty, especially for a sailor. Once he reached the height of the window, however, he could go no farther: it was too far to his left. All he could manage was to stretch across and catch a glimpse inside. What he saw horrified him so much that he nearly lost his grip and fell. It was then that the dreadful screams rang out through the night, waking the residents of the Rue Morgue. Madame L’Espanaye and her daughter, both in nightclothes, had apparently been sorting papers in the iron chest already mentioned. It had been wheeled into the centre of the room and stood open, its contents spread on the floor beside it. The victims must have been sitting with their backs to the window. Judging by the interval between the animal’s entry and the screams, they probably did not notice it immediately. They would naturally have assumed that the wind had swung the shutter closed.

As the sailor looked in, the enormous animal had grabbed Madame L’Espanaye by her hair, which hung loose because she had been combing it. It was waving the razor around her face, imitating the movements of a barber.

It was just then that his gaze, as well as my own, lighted upon the piece of parchment, which I took at the time for paper. Half of it lay beneath the sand, with one corner projecting. Close to the place of its discovery I noticed the remains of a hull, apparently belonging to a ship’s longboat. The wreck must have rested there for many years, since its likeness to the timbers of a boat was barely discernible.

‘Well, Jupiter gathered up the parchment, folded it round the beetle, and handed it to me. A little later we started homeward and encountered Lieutenant G—— on the way. I displayed the insect to him, and he begged permission to carry it to the fort. Once I agreed, he promptly slipped it into his waistcoat pocket without its covering, which I had kept in my hand while he examined it. Possibly he feared I might reconsider and wished to secure his prize immediately—you know his ardour for everything concerning Natural History. Meanwhile, without noticing what I did, I must have put the parchment into my own pocket.

‘You recollect that, upon going to the table to draw the beetle, I discovered no paper in its customary place. I tried the drawer, but there was none there either. I then felt through my pockets in hopes of finding an old letter, and my hand encountered the parchment. I describe so exactly how it reached my possession because these circumstances struck me with unusual force.

‘You will doubtless regard me as fanciful, but I had already perceived a sort of connection. Two links of an extensive chain were joined. A boat lay upon the seashore; nearby lay a piece of parchment—not paper—with the figure of a skull upon it. Naturally you will ask, “What connection is there?” My answer is that the skull, or death’s-head, is the familiar badge of pirates. Their death’s-head flag is raised whenever they engage in battle.

‘I have stressed that this fragment was parchment rather than paper. Parchment endures; it is almost indestructible. Things of small consequence are seldom committed to it, for it is far less convenient than paper for ordinary writing or drawing. That consideration hinted at a purpose, a significance, behind the death’s-head. I also took care to note the parchment’s shape. Though an accident had destroyed one corner, its original oblong form could still plainly be distinguished.’
